name: Intermaxillary fixation

card.summary: Holding the upper and lower jaws together with wires, elastics or screws, used after jaw surgery so repositioned bones heal where the surgeon placed them, which is how surgical jaw changes become a permanent look.
card.note: A surgical-recovery step with a liquid diet; modern rigid plate fixation has reduced how often and how long it is needed.

quick.overview:
Intermaxillary fixation (IMF), also called maxillomandibular fixation or jaw wiring, immobilises the upper and lower jaws against each other using arch bars, wires, elastics or screws. In appearance terms it is the recovery stage of jaw surgery: after procedures such as bimaxillary or genioplasty work that move the jaws, fixation keeps them in the planned position while bone heals.

It began as the jaw's equivalent of a cast for fractures. Since the 1980s, rigid internal plates have reduced how often prolonged wiring is needed after orthognathic surgery, though it remains in use in some cases and for fractures.
quick.how: A surgeon fits the fixation, typically in the operating room, and it usually stays for about four to six weeks, sometimes longer, during which the person eats a liquid diet. Elastics are often used instead of rigid wires in modern practice. Follow-up includes oral hygiene and staged return to normal eating.
quick.risks: Reported issues include difficulty eating and speaking, weight loss, oral hygiene problems, tooth damage, numbness, infection and healing problems. Airway protection matters, since vomiting is a concern while the jaws are fixed, so patients are given release instructions by their surgical team.

lead: Intermaxillary fixation, also called maxillomandibular fixation, is a technique that holds the upper and lower jaws together so that they cannot move. An oral surgeon attaches arch bars to both jaws and links them with wires or elastics, pressing the upper teeth against the lower ones.[1] It treats mandibular fractures and supports orthognathic (jaw-correcting) surgery.[1]

For people changing their faces, the relevance is the recovery phase of jaw surgery. Operations that set a recessed chin or jaw forward, or reposition the upper jaw, only deliver their look if the bones heal in the new position, and fixation was historically how that was ensured.[2] A review of sagittal split osteotomy notes that osteosynthesis with wires in the 1970s required strict intermaxillary fixation for six weeks, while rigid and semi-rigid fixation in the 1980s removed that need.[3]

The technique dates to antiquity: Grokipedia attributes early wiring of fractured jaws to Hippocrates, and it became standard for jaw fractures in the 20th century before rigid plates shifted it to an adjunct role.[2]

chain: Fixation holds the new position while bone heals
Surgical changes in jaw and chin projection are kept
angle.text: Fixation does not change the face itself. It is the immobilisation step that lets surgical jaw changes (such as a set-forward lower jaw) heal in the intended position, giving a more projected chin or jawline.

paras: Fixation is applied by attaching arch bars or screws to the teeth or bone of each jaw and linking them with wires or elastics, which keeps the upper teeth pressed against the lower teeth.[1] It acts as the equivalent of a cast for a fractured lower jaw.[1]
Usual duration is about four to six weeks, sometimes two to three months, and patients rely on a liquid diet during that time.[1]

Orthognathic surgery corrects jaw deformities, and fixation has been part of its stabilisation. A 2017 review of controversies in orthognathic surgery describes the move from prolonged intermaxillary fixation and wire osteosynthesis to rigid internal fixation, and the debate about which technique gives the most stable results.[4]

Retrognathia, a receding jaw, is usually corrected with orthodontics and surgery, most often a sagittal splitting osteotomy; a 1989 review noted that relapse was a formidable problem and that lag-screw fixation was very stable but required a facial incision.[5]

Clinical interest has also turned to making the device more comfortable. A randomized multicenter trial compared IMF screws with arch bars for mandibular condyle fractures and assessed patient quality of life, since arch bars were described as inconvenient and lowering quality of life.[6]
Grokipedia dates wiring of fractured jaws to Hippocrates and reports steel-wire fixation advances in the 19th century and wide use of arch bars and elastics in World War II.[2]

In the 1970s and early 1980s jaw wiring was also used for weight loss to enforce a liquid diet, and a 1980 study described it as a safe but ineffective means of controlling weight; patients in weight-loss studies often regained much of the weight after unwiring.[1] Wikipedia reports it continues in Nigeria and South Africa.[1]

Grokipedia lists tooth damage, numbness, bleeding, infection and improper bone healing as possible complications, and notes patients carry wire cutters for emergency release if vomiting or choking occurs.[2] The procedure is invasive and needs general anesthesia.[1]

Trials have compared fixation devices, such as arch bars with IMF screws and arch bars with embrasure wire, mostly in mandibular fracture patients.[6][7] A registered trial has also compared vertical ramus osteotomy with patient-specific fixation against maxillomandibular fixation for mandibular prognathism, with patient satisfaction as the outcome.[8]

timeline.event: Wire osteosynthesis after sagittal split osteotomy requires about six weeks of strict intermaxillary fixation.[3]
Jaw wiring is also used for weight loss.[1]
Rigid and semi-rigid fixation removes the need for IMF after sagittal split osteotomy.[3]
